lesson.title: The Oscilloscope Probe: Connecting Without Disturbing
lesson.summary: An oscilloscope probe carries a signal from the circuit under test to the scope's input, and the common 10x probe design trades signal amplitude for a much higher input impedance, adding a 9 megaohm series resistor that forms a 10:1 divider with the scope's own 1 megaohm input.
lesson.body:
You cannot connect a circuit directly to an oscilloscope's input with a bare wire and expect accurate results, especially for fast or sensitive signals, so the connection is made instead through a probe: a specialized cable with a spring loaded tip at one end and a connector matched to the scope's input at the other. The simplest kind, called a 1x probe, passes the signal through essentially unchanged, connecting the circuit directly to the scope's input, which is typically 1 megaohm of resistance in parallel with a small amount of capacitance.

The far more common design in general purpose use is the 10x probe, which deliberately adds a 9 megaohm resistor in series inside the probe tip itself. Combined with the scope's own 1 megaohm input resistance, this forms a resistive divider: 9 megaohms in series with 1 megaohm gives a 10:1 ratio, so only one tenth of the actual signal voltage reaches the scope's input circuitry, and the scope, or the probe's coding, which many scopes read automatically, multiplies the displayed reading by 10 to show the true value. If the true signal is 2 volts, the scope's input circuitry only ever sees 200 millivolts, but the display correctly shows 2 volts because it accounts for the 10x attenuation.

The reason this trade is worth making is impedance, not just accuracy of the number. Adding that 9 megaohm resistor raises the total resistance the probe presents to the circuit under test from 1 megaohm, a bare 1x connection, to 10 megaohms. A higher input impedance means the probe draws far less current from the circuit it is connected to, which matters because any current the probe does draw is current not doing what the circuit itself intended, subtly changing the very voltage you are trying to observe. This effect is called loading, and a 10x probe loads the circuit far less than a 1x connection does, at the cost of one tenth the signal reaching the scope, a cost that is easily undone by the scope's 10x multiplication as long as the probe and scope agree on that setting.
